LLMS.TXT GENERATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Build a valid llms.txt for your site

Paste a short list of your pages, a sitemap.xml, or point the CLI at a local Markdown docs tree — this assembles a correctly structured llms.txt file (the emerging convention that gives AI assistants a curated map of your site) and checks the result against the spec's own shape before you publish it.

Nothing is uploaded. Everything below runs in this browser and is never sent anywhere.

Build from a page list

Build from a sitemap.xml

Every URL lands under one "## Pages" section, titled by its own URL — edit titles afterward in the output, or use the page-list tab for per-link titles.

Validate an existing llms.txt

Result

Prefer a CLI, or generating this in CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it can walk a real Markdown docs tree or fetch a live sitemap directly (Node has no cross-origin restriction, unlike this page):

node cli.mjs --dir ./docs --title "Example Docs" --base-url https://example.com
node cli.mjs --sitemap https://example.com/sitemap.xml --title "Example Site"
node cli.mjs --urls-file ./urls.txt --title "Example Site" --out llms.txt
node cli.mjs --check ./llms.txt

Get cli.mjs and generator.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install.

Common questions

What is llms.txt?

An emerging, optional convention (see llmstxt.org) for a plain-text Markdown file at /llms.txt that gives an AI assistant a short, curated map of a site's most important pages — cheaper to read than crawling the whole site, and curated rather than everything a sitemap lists. It is not enforced by any browser or search engine; it is a convention some AI tools already read and more are adopting. More background: what llms.txt is for, and what it isn't.

Is this file generated correctly to spec?

The generator always produces the required shape — an H1 title, an optional blockquote summary, and Markdown link bullets grouped under "## Section" headings — and every build is run back through the same validator shown in tab 3, so you see any warning before you publish. What it can't know is whether you picked the right pages to include; that judgment stays yours.

Is my content uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page builds and validates entirely in your own browser and never sends what you paste anywhere. The CLI only reads local files, or fetches a URL you explicitly name (a sitemap.xml), and makes no other network call.

Where do I put the generated file?

Publish it at the root of your site as /llms.txt — the same level as /robots.txt — so it's reachable at https://yoursite.com/llms.txt.

Same convention, opposite job: AI Crawler Access Check checks whether your robots.txt actually lets named AI crawlers reach your site, and does a lightweight structural check of an llms.txt you already have — this tool builds one from scratch instead of grading one that exists.

Already have docs hosted somewhere, or thinking about moving them for a platform that builds llms.txt for you? This generator vs. a hosted docs platform's built-in llms.txt feature lays out that tradeoff.

Thinking about just typing the file yourself? This generator vs. writing llms.txt by hand covers what actually goes wrong when you do.

It produces a file matching the structural shape of the llmstxt.org convention — it does not guarantee any AI assistant reads or honors it, and it cannot judge whether the pages you chose to include are the right ones. vs-a-hosted-docs-platform.html.text:
← llms.txt Generator

This generator vs. a hosted docs platform's built-in llms.txt feature

Several documentation hosting platforms now generate an llms.txt automatically, as one feature of moving your whole docs site onto their platform. This free tool builds and validates the same spec-compliant file from docs you already have — hosted anywhere — with no migration and no recurring cost.

What each one is for

A hosted documentation platform that auto-generates llms.txt does so as one bundled feature of its whole pipeline: your content lives on that platform, and because it controls every step from authoring to publishing, it can regenerate the file automatically the moment a page changes. That convenience comes with the platform's own pricing, its own authoring format, and a migration of docs that may already live somewhere else.

This generator does not need your docs to live anywhere in particular. Paste a short page list, paste a sitemap.xml you already publish, or point the CLI at a local Markdown tree, and it produces a correctly structured llms.txt — plus a validator, in the same tool, for one you already have. Nothing is uploaded, there is no account, and nothing about your documentation has to move.

It exists because the two are answering different questions. "Where should our documentation be hosted" is a real decision with real tradeoffs that has nothing to do with one file. "Do we have a spec-correct llms.txt today" is a much narrower question, and this tool answers it for free without requiring the first decision at all. See what llms.txt is, and whether you need one for the background.

Common questions

Should I use this generator or switch to a hosted docs platform that builds llms.txt automatically?

Depends why you would be switching. Moving your whole documentation site to a new host is a large decision — pricing, migration effort, and lock-in to that platform's authoring format — that should be justified by more than one file. If you already publish docs, on any host or none at all, and just need a correctly structured llms.txt today, paste your existing sitemap.xml or a short page list into this generator for free — no migration required.

Does this tool keep my llms.txt updated automatically the way a hosted platform would?

Not on its own — the browser tool is a point-in-time build. A hosted docs platform that owns your whole publishing pipeline can regenerate the file the moment a page is added or removed, because it controls every step. This tool gets you the same automatic-on-deploy behavior a different way: wire the CLI's --dir or --sitemap mode into your own build or deploy script, and it regenerates on every push without migrating anything.

What does this generator's validator check that a hosted platform's built-in generator gets right automatically?

The structural shape the llmstxt.org convention actually requires: an H1 title, an optional blockquote summary, and Markdown link bullets grouped under "## Section" headings. A hosted platform's own generator gets this right by construction, since it controls the whole pipeline end to end. This tool checks the same shape explicitly instead, because it doesn't control your pipeline — you can paste any llms.txt, from any source, into the validator tab and get the identical structural check.

Why not just migrate to a docs platform that includes this feature?

Proportionality. Moving your documentation hosting to gain one auto-generated file is a large move if that file is the only feature you actually want, and it ties the file's freshness to staying on that vendor's platform going forward. This generator produces the identical structural file today, from documentation hosted wherever it already lives, at no cost and with nothing to migrate.

vs-writing-llms-txt-by-hand.html.text:
← llms.txt Generator

This generator vs. writing llms.txt by hand

Hand-writing an llms.txt means copying URLs into a text file and getting the Markdown shape right yourself — the exact link-bullet syntax, the ## Section grouping the spec expects — then remembering to update it every time a page is added or removed. This free tool builds and validates the same spec-compliant file from a pasted sitemap.xml, a short page list, or a local docs tree, and the CLI keeps it current automatically.

What actually goes wrong by hand

llms.txt looks like a plain text file, so it is tempting to just type one. Three specific things go wrong when you do, and none of them are judgment calls — they are mechanical slips that are easy to make once and never notice:

  • The link syntax. Each entry under a section has to be a real Markdown link bullet — - [Title](url): optional note — not a bare URL pasted on its own line. Drop a bracket or forget the leading - [ and the file still looks fine to read; it is just no longer the shape the spec describes.
  • The section grouping. The convention expects links grouped under ## Section headings, not one flat list. Nothing stops you from skipping the headings entirely, and a flat list is exactly what you get if you started by pasting a raw sitemap.xml in by hand, one <loc> per line.
  • Staying in sync. The file is a snapshot of whatever your docs looked like the day you wrote it. Add a page, rename one, or retire a section, and the hand-written file does not know — nothing forces you to reopen it, so it quietly drifts from what you actually publish.

This generator removes exactly those three failure points. It always emits the correct H1 title, optional blockquote summary, and Markdown link bullets grouped under ## Section headings, from a pasted page list, a pasted sitemap.xml, or — via the CLI — a local Markdown docs tree, and every build is checked against the same validator shown in the tool's third tab before you publish. For staying in sync, wire cli.mjs's --dir or --sitemap mode into your own build or deploy script and it regenerates from your current pages on every run, instead of from whatever you remembered to type in by hand.

What it does not do is pick which pages belong in the file — that judgment call is still yours, generator or not. See what llms.txt is, and whether you need one for the background, or this generator vs. a hosted docs platform's built-in llms.txt feature for the other comparison this venture publishes.

Writing it by handThis generator
Type each - [Title](url): note bullet yourself and hope you didn't drop a bracket.Paste a page list or sitemap; the Markdown link syntax is always correct.
Remember to group links under ## Section headings, or skip it and get a flat list.Sections come from the page-list tab's own ## Section lines, or one grouped "Pages" section from a sitemap.
No way to check the result except reading it over yourself.Every build runs back through the same validator you can also paste any llms.txt into directly.

Deciding which pages belong in the file.Still your call — this tool formats and validates, it does not curate.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, building and validating run in your browser, and nothing you paste is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

What actually goes wrong when you write llms.txt by hand?

Three things, all mechanical rather than judgment calls. The link bullets have to be exact Markdown — "- [Title](url): optional note" — and a missing bracket or a bare URL without the link syntax is easy to type past yourself. The pages need grouping under "## Section" headings, not a flat list, which the spec expects but nothing stops you from skipping. And the file has to be kept in sync as pages are added or removed, which nobody remembers to do by hand once it is not new anymore.

Isn't llms.txt just a short text file — why would I need a generator for it?

The content decisions — which pages matter, what to say about each one — are genuinely yours, and this tool does not make them for you. What it removes is the formatting risk: it always emits the required H1 title, optional blockquote summary, and Markdown link bullets grouped under "## Section" headings, and it validates the result against the same rules before you publish, so a typo'd bracket or an ungrouped link list is caught rather than shipped.

How do I keep llms.txt updated as my docs change, without redoing this by hand every time?

Wire cli.mjs's --dir (a local Markdown docs tree) or --sitemap (a local or live sitemap.xml) mode into your build or deploy script. It regenerates the file from your current pages on every run, so the file tracks what you actually publish instead of a snapshot from whenever you last remembered to edit it by hand.

I already have an llms.txt I wrote by hand — do I need to redo it?

Not necessarily. Paste it into this tool's validate tab first — it checks the same structural rules a generated file already satisfies, for free, with nothing uploaded. If it comes back clean, keep it; if it flags a missing section heading or a malformed link, you now know exactly what to fix instead of guessing.

what-is-llms-txt.html.text:
← Back to the llms.txt generator

What is llms.txt, and do you need one?

llms.txt is a proposal from Answer.AI (published by Jeremy Howard) for a plain-text Markdown file at /llms.txt that gives an AI assistant a short, curated map of a site's most useful pages. The convention is not a web standard, and no browser or search engine is required to read it — it exists because some AI tools already fetch it when they encounter it, and more documentation platforms (several static-site generators and docs hosts) have started publishing one by default.

How it differs from robots.txt and sitemap.xml

These three files answer different questions, and a site can have all three at once:

  • robots.txt — "which crawlers may fetch which paths." An access rule, not a content summary.
  • sitemap.xml — "every URL that exists and should be indexed." Exhaustive and machine-generated, not curated.
  • llms.txt — "the handful of pages that actually explain this site or product." Curated and short by design — the opposite of exhaustive.

If you already publish a sitemap with hundreds of URLs, llms.txt is not a second copy of it — pasting your whole sitemap in verbatim (which this tool's sitemap mode makes easy to do by accident) defeats the point. The page-list tab is the better starting point for most sites: hand-pick the pages that matter.

The shape the convention describes

# Site or Project Name

> One-sentence summary of what this is.

## Docs
- [Getting started](https://example.com/docs/start): what this page covers
- [API reference](https://example.com/docs/api)

## Optional
- [Changelog](https://example.com/changelog)

An H1 title, an optional blockquote summary, then any number of "## Section" headings each holding Markdown link bullets. The convention's own suggestion is an "## Optional" section at the end for links that can be skipped first if an assistant has limited context to spend — this generator lets you name any section, including that one.

A docs site with a few hundred pages, several formats of the same content, or a lot of historical/versioned material is exactly the case the convention was written for.

Keeping it current

An llms.txt that links to a page you deleted, or omits a major new doc, is worse than not having one — the same "a guard nobody runs is worth less than no guard" problem any generated artifact has. If you regenerate it from a sitemap or docs tree on every deploy (the CLI is built for exactly that — see the main page), it can't go stale the way a hand-maintained one will.

Frequently asked questions

Does llms.txt replace robots.txt or sitemap.xml?

No. robots.txt controls crawler access, sitemap.xml lists every URL that should be indexed, and llms.txt is a curated, short map of the pages that actually explain a site or product — a different job from either, and a site can have all three at once.

Do you need one?

It helps most on documentation sites, API references, and developer-facing tools where there is real depth to summarize and a real audience (including AI coding assistants) that benefits from a shortcut past the marketing pages. A five-page brochure site has little to gain.

What should not go in it?

Everything your sitemap already lists is the wrong scope — llms.txt is meant to be curated and short, not exhaustive. Leave out marketing pages, legal boilerplate, and anything not meant to inform an assistant answering a question about the product.

Build one now →

No warranty. This page is informational, not a specification. Confirm anything load-bearing against llmstxt.org itself, which may change.
